entries.79ae433336dfd9960de1b6a1676d0e0a76779745: <div sID="gen992" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="29" osisID="Gen.29" sID="Gen.29"/> <div eID="gen992" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen993" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen994" type="x-p"/> This chapter gives us an account of God's providences concerning Jacob, pursuant to the promises made to him in the foregoing chapter. I. How he was brought in safety to his journey's end, and directed to his relations there, who bade him welcome, <reference osisRef="Gen.29.1-Gen.29.14">ver. 1-14</reference>. II. How he was comfortably disposed of in marriage, <reference osisRef="Gen.29.15-Gen.29.30">ver. 15-30</reference>. III. How his family was built up in the birth of four sons, <reference osisRef="Gen.29.31-Gen.29.35">ver. 31-35</reference>. The affairs of princes and mighty nations that were then in being are not recorded in the book of God, but are left to be buried in oblivion; while these small domestic concerns of holy Jacob are particularly recorded with their minute circumstances, that they may be in everlasting remembrance. For "the memory of the just is blessed."
entries.4041e919211d95a2e1cc31c17e8b388c89ce1b50: <div eID="gen994" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen993" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Jacob's Arrival at Padan-aram. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1760.)</title> <div sID="gen995" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Then Jacob went on his journey, and came into the land of the people of the east. <hi type="super">2</hi> And he looked, and behold a well in the field, and, lo, there <hi type="italic">were</hi> three flocks of sheep lying by it; for out of that well they watered the flocks: and a great stone <hi type="italic">was</hi> upon the well's mouth. <hi type="super">3</hi> And thither were all the flocks gathered: and they rolled the stone from the well's mouth, and watered the sheep, and put the stone again upon the well's mouth in his place. <hi type="super">4</hi> And Jacob said unto them, My brethren, whence <hi type="italic">be</hi> ye? And they said, Of Haran <hi type="italic">are</hi> we. <hi type="super">5</hi> And he said unto them, Know ye Laban the son of Nahor? And they said, We know <hi type="italic">him.</hi> <hi type="super">6</hi> And he said unto them, <hi type="italic">Is</hi> he well? And they said, <hi type="italic">He is</hi> well: and, behold, Rachel his daughter cometh with the sheep. 7 And he said, Lo, <hi type="italic">it is</hi> yet high day, neither <hi type="italic">is it</hi> time that the cattle should be gathered together: water ye the sheep, and go <hi type="italic">and</hi> feed <hi type="italic">them.</hi> <hi type="super">8</hi> And they said, We cannot, until all the flocks be gathered together, and <hi type="italic">till</hi> they roll the stone from the well's mouth; then we water the sheep. <div eID="gen995" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen996" type="x-p"/> All the stages Israel's march to Canaan are distinctly noticed, but no particular journal is kept of Jacob's expedition further than Beth-el; no, he had no more such happy nights as he had at Beth-el, no more such visions of the Almighty. That was intended for a feast; he must not expect it to be his daily bread. But, 1. We are here told how cheerfully he proceeded in his journey after the sweet communion he had with God at Beth-el: <hi type="italic">Then Jacob lifted up his feet;</hi> so the margin reads it, <reference osisRef="Gen.29.1">v. 1</reference>. Then he went on with cheerfulness and alacrity, not burdened with his cares, nor cramped with his fears, being assured of God's gracious presence with him. Note, After the visions we have had of God, and the vows we have made to him in solemn ordinances, we should run the way of his commandments with enlarged hearts, <reference osisRef="Heb.12.1">Heb. xii. 1</reference>. 2. How happily he arrived at his journey's end. Providence brought him to the very field where his uncle's flocks were to be watered, and there he met with Rachel, who was to be his wife. Observe, (1.) The divine Providence is to be acknowledged in all the little circumstances which concur to make a journey, or other undertaking, comfortable and successful. If, when we are at a loss, we meet seasonably with those that can direct us—if we meet with a disaster, and those are at hand that will help us—we must not say that it was by chance, nor that fortune therein favoured us, but that it was by Providence, and that God therein favoured us. Our ways are ways of pleasantness, if we continually acknowledge God in them. (2.) Those that have flocks must look well to them, and be diligent to know their state, <reference osisRef="Prov.27.23">Prov. xxvii. 23</reference>. What is here said of the constant care of the shepherds concerning their sheep (<reference osisRef="Gen.29.2-Gen.29.3">v. 2, 3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.29.7">7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.29.8">8</reference>) may serve to illustrate the tender concern which our Lord Jesus, the great Shepherd of the sheep, has for his flock, the church; for he is the good Shepherd, that knows his sheep, and is known of them, <reference osisRef="John.10.14">John x. 14</reference>. The stone at the well's mouth, which is so often mentioned here, was either to secure their property in it (for water was scarce, it was not there <hi type="italic">usus communis aquarum—for every one's use</hi>), or it was to save the well from receiving damage from the heat of the sun, or from any spiteful hand, or to prevent the lambs of the flock from being drowned in it. (3.) Separate interests should not take us from joint and mutual help; when all the shepherds came together with their flocks, then, like loving neighbours, at watering-time, they watered their flocks together. (4.) It becomes us to speak civilly and respectfully to strangers. Though Jacob was no courtier, but a plain man, dwelling in tents, and a stranger to compliment, yet he addresses himself very obligingly to the people he met with, and calls them his <hi type="italic">brethren,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.29.4">v. 4</reference>. The law of kindness in the tongue has a commanding power, <reference osisRef="Prov.31.26">Prov. xxxi. 26</reference>. Some think he calls them brethren because they were of the same trade, shepherds like him. Though he was now upon his preferment, he was not ashamed of his occupation. (5.) Those that show respect have usually respect shown to them. As Jacob was civil to these strangers, so he found them civil to him. When he undertook to teach them how to despatch their business (<reference osisRef="Gen.29.7">v. 7</reference>), they did not bid him meddle with his own concerns and let them alone; but, though he was a stranger, they gave him the reason of their delay, <reference osisRef="Gen.29.8">v. 8</reference>. Those that are neighbourly and friendly shall have neighbourly and friendly usage.
entries.6ea01e091e564c448192435fc2a05c0276b34a8a: <div eID="gen996" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Rachel's Humility and Industry. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1760.)</title> <div sID="gen997" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> And while he yet spake with them, Rachel came with her father's sheep: for she kept them. <hi type="super">10</hi> And it came to pass, when Jacob saw Rachel the daughter of Laban his mother's brother, and the sheep of Laban his mother's brother, that Jacob went near, and rolled the stone from the well's mouth, and watered the flock of Laban his mother's brother. <hi type="super">11</hi> And Jacob kissed Rachel, and lifted up his voice, and wept. <hi type="super">12</hi> And Jacob told Rachel that he <hi type="italic">was</hi> her father's brother, and that he <hi type="italic">was</hi> Rebekah's son: and she ran and told her father. <hi type="super">13</hi> And it came to pass, when Laban heard the tidings of Jacob his sister's son, that he ran to meet him, and embraced him, and kissed him, and brought him to his house. And he told Laban all these things. <hi type="super">14</hi> And Laban said to him, Surely thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> my bone and my flesh. And he abode with him the space of a month. <div eID="gen997" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen998" type="x-p"/> Here we see, 1. Rachel's humility and industry: <hi type="italic">She kept her father's sheep</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.29.9">v. 9</reference>), that is, she took the care of them, having servants under her that were employed about them. Rachel's name signifies <hi type="italic">a sheep.</hi> Note, Honest useful labour is that which nobody needs be ashamed of, nor ought it to be a hindrance to any one's preferment. 2. Jacob's tenderness and affection. When he understood that this was his kinswoman (probably he had heard of her name before), knowing what his errand was into that country, we may suppose it struck his mind immediately that this must be his wife. Being already smitten with her ingenuous comely face (though it was probably sun-burnt, and she was in the homely dress of a shepherdess), he is wonderfully officious, and anxious to serve her (<reference osisRef="Gen.29.10">v. 10</reference>), and addresses himself to her with tears of joy and kisses of love, <reference osisRef="Gen.29.11">v. 11</reference>. She runs with all haste to tell her father; for she will by no means entertain her kinsman's address without her father's knowledge and approbation, <reference osisRef="Gen.29.12">v. 12</reference>. These mutual respects, at their first interview, were good presages of their being a happy couple. 3. Providence made that which seemed contingent and fortuitous to give speedy satisfaction to Jacob's mind, as soon as ever he came to the place which he was bound for. Abraham's servant, when he came upon a similar errand, met with similar encouragement. Thus God guides his people with his eye, <reference osisRef="Ps.32.8">Ps. xxxii. 8</reference>. It is a groundless conceit which some of the Jewish writers have, that Jacob, when he kissed Rachel, wept because he had been set upon in his journey by Eliphaz the eldest son of Esau, at the command of his father, and robbed of all his money and jewels, which his mother had given him when she sent him away. It was plain that it was his passion for Rachel, and the surprise of this happy meeting, that drew these tears from his eyes. 4. Laban, though none of the best-humoured men, bade him welcome, was satisfied in the account he gave of himself, and of the reason of his coming in such poor circumstances. While we avoid the extreme, on the one hand, of being foolishly credulous, we must take heed of falling into the other extreme, of being uncharitably jealous and suspicious. Laban owned him for his kinsman: <hi type="italic">Thou art my bone and my flesh,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.29.14">v. 14</reference>. Note, Those are hard-hearted indeed that are unkind to their relations, and that <hi type="italic">hide themselves from their own flesh,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.58.7">Isa. lviii. 7</reference>.
entries.cf90ee9d5e9f3d32c48f485abd6e83262c51d403: <div eID="gen998" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Jacob's Marriage. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1753.)</title> <div sID="gen999" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> And Laban said unto Jacob, Because thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> my brother, shouldest thou therefore serve me for nought? tell me, what <hi type="italic">shall</hi> thy wages <hi type="italic">be?</hi> <hi type="super">16</hi> And Laban had two daughters: the name of the elder <hi type="italic">was</hi> Leah, and the name of the younger <hi type="italic">was</hi> Rachel. <hi type="super">17</hi> Leah <hi type="italic">was</hi> tender eyed; but Rachel was beautiful and well favoured. <hi type="super">18</hi> And Jacob loved Rachel; and said, I will serve thee seven years for Rachel thy younger daughter. <hi type="super">19</hi> And Laban said, <hi type="italic">It is</hi> better that I give her to thee, than that I should give her to another man: abide with me. <hi type="super">20</hi> And Jacob served seven years for Rachel; and they seemed unto him <hi type="italic">but</hi> a few days, for the love he had to her. 21 And Jacob said unto Laban, Give <hi type="italic">me</hi> my wife, for my days are fulfilled, that I may go in unto her. <hi type="super">22</hi> And Laban gathered together all the men of the place, and made a feast. 23 And it came to pass in the evening, that he took Leah his daughter, and brought her to him; and he went in unto her. <hi type="super">24</hi> And Laban gave unto his daughter Leah Zilpah his maid <hi type="italic">for</hi> a handmaid. <hi type="super">25</hi> And it came to pass, that in the morning, behold, it <hi type="italic">was</hi> Leah: and he said to Laban, What <hi type="italic">is</hi> this thou hast done unto me? did not I serve with thee for Rachel? wherefore then hast thou beguiled me? <hi type="super">26</hi> And Laban said, It must not be so done in our country, to give the younger before the firstborn. <hi type="super">27</hi> Fulfil her week, and we will give thee this also for the service which thou shalt serve with me yet seven other years. <hi type="super">28</hi> And Jacob did so, and fulfilled her week: and he gave him Rachel his daughter to wife also. <hi type="super">29</hi> And Laban gave to Rachel his daughter Bilhah his handmaid to be her maid. <hi type="super">30</hi> And he went in also unto Rachel, and he loved also Rachel more than Leah, and served with him yet seven other years. <div eID="gen999" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1000" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. The fair contract made between Laban and Jacob, during the month that Jacob spent there as a guest, <reference osisRef="Gen.29.14">v. 14</reference>. It seems he was not idle, nor did he spend his time in sport and pastime; but like a man of business, though he had no stock of his own, he applied himself to serve his uncle, as he had begun (<reference osisRef="Gen.29.10">v. 10</reference>) when he <hi type="italic">watered his flock.</hi> Note, Wherever we are, it is good to be employing ourselves in some useful business, which will turn to a good account to ourselves or others. Laban, it seems, was so taken with Jacob's ingenuity and industry about his flocks that he was desirous he should continue with him, and very fairly reasons thus: "<hi type="italic">Because thou art my brother, shouldst thou therefore serve me for nought?</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.29.15">v. 15</reference>. No, what reason for that?" If Jacob be so respectful to his uncle as to give him his service without demanding any consideration for it, yet Laban will not be so unjust to his nephew as to take advantage either of his necessity or of his good-nature. Note, Inferior relations must not be imposed upon; if it be their duty to serve us, it is our duty to reward them. Now Jacob had a fair opportunity to make known to Laban the affection he had for his daughter Rachel; and, having no worldly goods in his hand with which to endow her, he promises him seven years' service, upon condition that, at the end of the seven years, he would bestow her upon him for his wife. It appears by computation that Jacob was now seventy-seven years old when he bound himself apprentice for a wife, <hi type="italic">and for a wife he kept sheep,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.12.12">Hos. xii. 12</reference>. His posterity are there reminded of it long afterwards, as an instance of the meanness of their origin: probably Rachel was young, and scarcely marriageable, when Jacob first came, which made him the more willing to stay for her till his seven years' service had expired. <div eID="gen1000" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1001" type="x-p"/> II. Jacob's honest performance of his part of the bargain, <reference osisRef="Gen.29.20">v. 20</reference>. He served seven years for Rachel. If Rachel still continued to keep her father's sheep (as she did, <reference osisRef="Gen.29.9">v. 9</reference>), his innocent and religious conversation with her, while they kept the flocks, could not but increase their mutual acquaintance and affection (Solomon's song of love is a pastoral); if she now left it off, his easing her of that care was very obliging. Jacob honestly served out his seven years, and did not forfeit his indentures, though he was old; nay, he served them cheerfully: <hi type="italic">They seemed to him but a few days, for the love he had to her,</hi> as if it were more his desire to earn her than to have her. Note, Love makes long and hard services short and easy; hence we read of <hi type="italic">the labour of love,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.6.10">Heb. vi. 10</reference>. If we know how to value the happiness of heaven, the sufferings of this present time will be as nothing to us in comparison of it. An age of work will be but as a few days to those that love God and long for Christ's appearing. <div eID="gen1001" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1002" type="x-p"/> III. The base cheat which Laban put upon him when he was out of his time: he put Leah into his arms instead of Rachel, <reference osisRef="Gen.29.23">v. 23</reference>. This was Laban's sin; he wronged both Jacob and Rachel, whose affections, doubtless, were engaged to each other, and, if (as some say) Leah was herein no better than an adulteress, it was no small wrong to her too. But it was Jacob's affliction, a damp to the mirth of the marriage-feast, when in the morning behold it was Leah, <reference osisRef="Gen.29.25">v. 25</reference>. It is easy to observe here how Jacob was paid in his own coin. He had cheated his own father when he pretended to be Esau, and now his father-in-law cheated him. Herein, how unrighteous soever Laban was, the Lord was righteous; as <reference osisRef="Judg.1.7">Judges i. 7</reference>. Even the righteous, if they take a false step, are sometimes thus recompensed on the earth. Many that are not, like Jacob, disappointed in the person, soon find themselves, as much to their grief, disappointed in the character. The choice of that relation therefore, on both sides, ought to be made with good advice and consideration, that, if there should be a disappointment, it may not be aggravated by a consciousness of mismanagement. <div eID="gen1002" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1003" type="x-p"/> IV. The excuse and atonement Laban made for the cheat. 1. The excuse was frivolous: <hi type="italic">It must not be so done in our country,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.29.26">v. 26</reference>. We have reason to think there was no such custom of his country as he pretends; only he banters Jacob with it, and laughs at his mistake. Note, Those that can do wickedly and then think to turn it off with a jest, though they may deceive themselves and others, will find at last that God is not mocked. But if there had been such a custom, and he had resolved to observe it, he should have told Jacob so when he undertook to serve him for his younger daughter. Note, As saith the proverb of the ancients, <hi type="italic">Wickedness proceeds from the wicked,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.24.13">1 Sam. xxiv. 13</reference>. Those that deal with treacherous men must expect to be dealt treacherously with. 2. His compounding the matter did but make bad worse: <hi type="italic">We will give thee this also,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.29.27">v. 27</reference>. Hereby he drew Jacob into the sin, and snare, and disquiet, of multiplying wives, which remains a blot in his escutcheon, and will be so to the end of the world. Honest Jacob did not design it, but to have kept as true to Rachel as his father had done to Rebekah. He that had lived without a wife to the eighty-fourth year of his age could then have been very well content with one; but Laban, to dispose of his two daughters without portions, and to get seven years' service more out of Jacob, thus imposes upon him, and draws him into such a strait by his fraud, that (the matter not being yet settled, as it was afterwards by the divine law, <reference osisRef="Lev.18.18">Lev. xviii. 18</reference>, and more fully since by our Saviour, <reference osisRef="Matt.19.5">Matt. xix. 5</reference>) he had some colourable reasons for marrying them both. He could not refuse Rachel, for he had espoused her; still less could he refuse Leah, for he had married her; and therefore Jacob must <hi type="italic">be content, and take two talents,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Kgs.5.23">2 Kings v. 23</reference>. Note, One sin is commonly the inlet of another. Those that go in by one door of wickedness seldom find their way out but by another. The polygamy of the patriarchs was, in some measure, excusable in them, because, though there was a reason against it as ancient as Adam's marriage (<reference osisRef="Mal.2.15">Mal. ii. 15</reference>), yet there was no express command against it; it was in them a sin of ignorance. It was not the product of any sinful lust, but for the building up of the church, which was the good that Providence brought out of it; but it will by no means justify the like practice now, when God's will is plainly made known, that one man and one woman only must be joined together, <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.2">1 Cor. vii. 2</reference>. The having of many wives suits well enough with the carnal sensual spirit of the Mahomedan imposture, which allows it; but we have not so learned Christ. Dr. Lightfoot makes Leah and Rachel to be figures of the two churches, the Jews under the law and the Gentiles under the gospel: the younger the more beautiful, and more in the thoughts of Christ when he came in the form of a servant; but he other, like Leah, first embraced: yet in this the allegory does not hold, that the Gentiles, the younger, were more fruitful, <reference osisRef="Gal.4.27">Gal. iv. 27</reference>.
entries.2e4c289db42543d9db2afd7e1972704a0830c13c: <div eID="gen1003" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Increase of Jacob's Family. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1749.)</title> <div sID="gen1004" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">31</hi> And when the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> saw that Leah <hi type="italic">was</hi> hated, he opened her womb: but Rachel <hi type="italic">was</hi> barren. <hi type="super">32</hi> And Leah conceived, and bare a son, and she called his name Reuben: for she said, Surely the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath looked upon my affliction; now therefore my husband will love me. <hi type="super">33</hi> And she conceived again, and bare a son; and said, Because the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath heard that I <hi type="italic">was</hi> hated, he hath therefore given me this <hi type="italic">son</hi> also: and she called his name Simeon. <hi type="super">34</hi> And she conceived again, and bare a son; and said, Now this time will my husband be joined unto me, because I have born him three sons: therefore was his name called Levi. <hi type="super">35</hi> And she conceived again, and bare a son: and she said, Now will I praise the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : therefore she called his name Judah; and left bearing. <div eID="gen1004" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1005" type="x-p"/> We have here the birth of four of Jacob's sons, all by Leah. Observe, 1. That Leah, who was less beloved, was blessed with children, when Rachel was denied that blessing, <reference osisRef="Gen.29.31">v. 31</reference>. See how Providence, in dispensing its gifts, observes a proportion, to keep the balance even, setting crosses and comforts one over-against another, that none may be either too much elevated or too much depressed. Rachel wants children, but she is blessed with her husband's love; Leah wants that, but she is fruitful. Thus it was between Elkana's two wives (<reference osisRef="1Sam.1.5">1 Sam. i. 5</reference>); for the Lord is wise and righteous. <hi type="italic">When the Lord saw that Leah was hated,</hi> that is, loved less than Rachel, in which sense it is required that we hate father and mother, in comparison with Christ (<reference osisRef="Luke.14.26">Luke xiv. 26</reference>), then the Lord granted her a child, which was a rebuke to Jacob, for making so great a difference between those that he was equally related to,—a check to Rachel, who perhaps insulted over her sister upon that account,—and a comfort to Leah, that she might not be overwhelmed with the contempt put upon her: thus <hi type="italic">God giveth abundant honour to that which lacked,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.24">1 Cor. xii. 24</reference>. 2. The names she gave her children were expressive of her respectful regards both to God and to her husband. (1.) She appears very ambitious of her husband's love: she reckoned the want of it her affliction (<reference osisRef="Gen.29.32">v. 32</reference>); not upbraiding him with it as his fault, nor reproaching him for it, and so making herself uneasy to him, but laying it to heart as her grief, which yet she had reason to bear with the more patience because she herself was consenting to the fraud by which she became his wife; and we may well bear that trouble with patience which we bring upon ourselves by our own sin and folly. She promised herself that the children she bore him would gain her the interest she desired in his affections. She called her first-born <hi type="italic">Reuben</hi> (<hi type="italic">see a son</hi>), with this pleasant thought, <hi type="italic">Now will my husband love me;</hi> and her third son <hi type="italic">Levi</hi> (<hi type="italic">joined</hi>), with this expectation, <hi type="italic">Now will my husband by joined unto me,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.29.34">v. 34</reference>. Mutual affection is both the duty and comfort of that relation; and yoke-fellows should study to recommend themselves to each other, <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.33-1Cor.7.34">1 Cor. vii. 33, 34</reference>. (2.) She thankfully acknowledges the kind providence of God in it: <hi type="italic">The Lord hath looked upon my affliction,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.29.32">v. 32</reference>. "<hi type="italic">The Lord hath heard,</hi> that is, taken notice of it, <hi type="italic">that I was hated</hi> (for our afflictions, as they are before God's eyes, so they have a cry in his ears), <hi type="italic">he has therefore given me this son.</hi>" Note, Whatever we have that contributes either to our support and comfort under our afflictions or to our deliverance from them, God must be owned in it, especially his pity and tender mercy. Her fourth she called <hi type="italic">Judah</hi> (<hi type="italic">praise</hi>), saying, <hi type="italic">Now will I praise the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.29.35">v. 35</reference>. And this was he of whom, as concerning the flesh, Christ came. Note, [1.] Whatever is the matter of our rejoicing ought to be the matter of our thanksgiving. Fresh favours should quicken us to praise God for former favours. <hi type="italic">Now will I praise the Lord</hi> more and better than I have done. [2.] All our praises must centre in Christ, both as the matter of them and as the Mediator of them. He descended from him whose name was praise, for he is our praise. Is Christ formed in my heart? <hi type="italic">Now will I praise the Lord.</hi>  <chapter eID="Gen.29"/> <div eID="gen1005" type="x-p"/>

entries.801f2666540147120ce9c231183d3046206c5b63: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv313"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 29</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Gen.29.1-Gen.29.35">Ge 29:1-35</reference>. The Well of Haran.</title> <div sID="gen495" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv313"/><hi type="bold">1. Then Jacob went, &c.--</hi>Hebrew, "lifted up his feet." He resumed his way next morning with a light heart and elastic step after the vision of the ladder; for tokens of the divine favor tend to quicken the discharge of duty (<reference osisRef="Neh.8.10">Ne 8:10</reference>).<div eID="gen495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen496" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and came into the land, &c.--</hi>Mesopotamia and the whole region beyond the Euphrates are by the sacred writers designated "the East" (<reference osisRef="Judg.6.3">Jud 6:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.30">1Ki 4:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.1.3">Job 1:3</reference>). Between the first and the second clause of this verse is included a journey of four hundred miles. <div eID="gen496" type="x-p"/>
entries.646615381eeeb775db2f40d6b8bc6da31d2102b5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv314"/><div sID="gen497" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv314"/><hi type="bold">2. And he looked, &c.--</hi>As he approached the place of his destination, he, according to custom, repaired to the well adjoining the town where he would obtain an easy introduction to his relatives. <div eID="gen497" type="x-p"/>
entries.03ffebdd0b4eb6c5628cb97f5c05ea839a7874a1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv315"/><div sID="gen498" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv315"/><hi type="bold">3. thither were all the flocks gathered; and a stone, &c.--</hi>In Arabia, owing to the shifting sands and in other places, owing to the strong evaporation, the mouth of a well is generally covered, especially when it is private property. Over many is laid a broad, thick, flat stone, with a round hole cut in the middle, forming the mouth of the cistern. This hole is covered with a heavy stone which it would require two or three men to roll away. Such was the description of the well at Haran. <div eID="gen498" type="x-p"/>
entries.756ee847abeaf40c8358d59384f1d7d796c02e78: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv316"/><div sID="gen499" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv316"/><hi type="bold">4. Jacob said, My brethren--</hi>Finding from the shepherds who were reposing there with flocks and who all belonged to Haran, that his relatives in Haran were well and that one of the family was shortly expected, he enquired why they were idling the best part of the day there instead of watering their flocks and sending them back to pasture. <div eID="gen499" type="x-p"/>
entries.3c8c761b842c21543b268c0c0fd2cee1f36e1561: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv317"/><div sID="gen500" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv317"/><hi type="bold">8. They said, We cannot, until all the flocks be gathered--</hi>In order to prevent the consequences of too frequent exposure in places where water is scarce, the well is not only covered, but it is customary to have all the flocks collected round it before the covering is removed in presence of the owner or one of his representatives; and it was for this reason that those who were reposing at the well of Haran with the three flocks were waiting the arrival of Rachel. <div eID="gen500" type="x-p"/>
entries.e5b2e356dd272900d336bb2bdf0b80dd356b7b60: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv318"/><div sID="gen501" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv318"/><hi type="bold">9-11. While he yet spake with them, Rachel came--</hi>Among the pastoral tribes the young unmarried daughters of the greatest sheiks tend the flocks, going out at sunrise and continuing to watch their fleecy charges till sunset. Watering them, which is done twice a day, is a work of time and labor, and Jacob rendered no small service in volunteering his aid to the young shepherdess. The interview was affecting, the reception welcome, and Jacob forgot all his toils in the society of his Mesopotamian relatives. Can we doubt that he returned thanks to God for His goodness by the way? <div eID="gen501" type="x-p"/>
entries.8278b0a80259a4704e9a14e5e6609f7ac1cc2c17: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv319"/><div sID="gen502" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv319"/><hi type="bold">12. Jacob told Rachel, &c.--</hi>According to the practice of the East, the term "brother" is extended to remote degrees of relationship, as uncle, cousin, or nephew. <div eID="gen502" type="x-p"/>
entries.b82362da6fb74936a8c05056b095f95bb3d302d5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv320"/><div sID="gen503" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv320"/><hi type="bold">14-20. he abode a month--</hi>Among pastoral people a stranger is freely entertained for three days; on the fourth day he is expected to tell his name and errand; and if he prolongs his stay after that time, he must set his hand to work in some way, as may be agreed upon. A similar rule obtained in Laban's establishment, and the wages for which his nephew engaged to continue in his employment was the hand of Rachel. <div eID="gen503" type="x-p"/>
entries.ba85c85e20fb4ac10b5997eca89c86d7e04d5f08: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv323"/><div sID="gen507" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv323"/><hi type="bold">21. Jacob said, Give me my wife--</hi>At the expiry of the stipulated term the marriage festivities were held. But an infamous fraud was practised on Jacob, and on his showing a righteous indignation, the usage of the country was pleaded in excuse. No plea of kindred should ever be allowed to come in opposition to the claim of justice. But this is often overlooked by the selfish mind of man, and fashion or custom rules instead of the will of God. This was what Laban did, as he said, "It must not be so done in our country, to give the younger before the first-born." But, then, if that were the prevailing custom of society at Haran, he should have apprized his nephew of it at an early period in an honorable manner. This, however, is too much the way with the people of the East still. The duty of marrying an elder daughter before a younger, the tricks which parents take to get off an elder daughter that is plain or deformed and in which they are favored by the long bridal veil that entirely conceals her features all the wedding day, and the prolongation for a week of the marriage festivities among the greater sheiks, are accordant with the habits of the people in Arabia and Armenia in the present day. <div eID="gen507" type="x-p"/>
entries.cdbfa49190ff191b477acaec97a1dd99fb7e4788: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv324"/><div sID="gen508" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv324"/><hi type="bold">28. gave him Rachel also--</hi>It is evident that the marriage of both sisters took place nearly about the same time, and that such a connection was then allowed, though afterwards prohibited (<reference osisRef="Lev.18.18">Le 18:18</reference>). <div eID="gen508" type="x-p"/>
entries.f5497ab506cfba23bfea7c8e615d800d059dc927: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv325"/><div sID="gen509" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv325"/><hi type="bold">29. gave to Rachel his daughter Bilhah to be her maid--</hi>A father in good circumstances still gives his daughter from his household a female slave, over whom the young wife, independently of her husband, has the absolute control. <div eID="gen509" type="x-p"/>
entries.6091e92a14f8a976dd3d4fab60d583f005b97612: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv326"/><div sID="gen510" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv326"/><hi type="bold">31. Leah ... hated--</hi>that is, not loved so much as she ought to have been. Her becoming a mother ensured her rising in the estimation both of her husband and of society. <div eID="gen510" type="x-p"/>
entries.8fba0deb7bdcf413c83d3e5d4b4da64960db35b2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv327"/><div sID="gen511" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv327"/><hi type="bold">32-35. son ... his name Reuben--</hi>Names were also significant; and those which Leah gave to her sons were expressive of her varying feelings of thankfulness or joy, or allusive to circumstances in the history of the family. There was piety and wisdom in attaching a signification to names, as it tended to keep the bearer in remembrance of his duty and the claims of God. <chapter eID="Gen.29"/>

entries.818a0bdc81aa9b12bb82381d1cf290f38961d0af: <div eID="gen1391" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen1392" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen1393" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen1393" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen1392" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen1394" type="x-p"/> Jacob proceeds on his journey, <reference osisRef="Gen.29.1">Gen 29:1</reference>. Comes to a well where the flocks of his uncle Laban, as well as those of several others, were usually watered, <reference osisRef="Gen.29.2">Gen 29:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.29.3">Gen 29:3</reference>. Inquires from the shepherds concerning Laban and his family, <reference osisRef="Gen.29.4-Gen.29.6">Gen 29:4-6</reference>. While they are conversing about watering the sheep, <reference osisRef="Gen.29.7">Gen 29:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.29.8">Gen 29:8</reference>, Rachel arrives, <reference osisRef="Gen.29.9">Gen 29:9</reference>. He assists her to water her flock, <reference osisRef="Gen.29.10">Gen 29:10</reference>; makes himself known unto her, <reference osisRef="Gen.29.11">Gen 29:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.29.12">Gen 29:12</reference>. She hastens home and communicates the tidings of Jacob's arrival to her father, <reference osisRef="Gen.29.12">Gen 29:12</reference>. Laban hastens to the well, embraces Jacob, and brings him home, <reference osisRef="Gen.29.13">Gen 29:13</reference>. After a month's stay, Laban proposes to give Jacob wages, <reference osisRef="Gen.29.14">Gen 29:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.29.15">Gen 29:15</reference>. Leah and Rachel described, <reference osisRef="Gen.29.16">Gen 29:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.29.17">Gen 29:17</reference>. Jacob proposes to serve seven years for Rachel, <reference osisRef="Gen.29.18">Gen 29:18</reference>. Laban consents, <reference osisRef="Gen.29.19">Gen 29:19</reference>. When the seven years were fulfilled, Jacob demands his wife, <reference osisRef="Gen.29.20">Gen 29:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.29.21">Gen 29:21</reference>. Laban makes a marriage feast, <reference osisRef="Gen.29.22">Gen 29:22</reference>; and in the evening substitutes Leah for Rachel, to whom he gives Zilpah for handmaid, <reference osisRef="Gen.29.23">Gen 29:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.29.24">Gen 29:24</reference>. Jacob discovers the fraud, and upbraids Laban, <reference osisRef="Gen.29.25">Gen 29:25</reference>. He excuses himself, <reference osisRef="Gen.29.26">Gen 29:26</reference>; and promises to give him Rachel for another seven years of service, <reference osisRef="Gen.29.27">Gen 29:27</reference>. After abiding a week with Leah, he receives Rachel for wife, to whom Laban gives Bilhah for handmaid, <reference osisRef="Gen.29.28">Gen 29:28</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.29.29">Gen 29:29</reference>. Jacob loves Rachel more than Leah, and serves seven years for her, <reference osisRef="Gen.29.30">Gen 29:30</reference>. Leah being despised, the Lord makes her fruitful, while Rachel continues barren, <reference osisRef="Gen.29.31">Gen 29:31</reference>. Leah bears Reuben, <reference osisRef="Gen.29.32">Gen 29:32</reference>, and Simeon, <reference osisRef="Gen.29.33">Gen 29:33</reference>, and Levi, <reference osisRef="Gen.29.34">Gen 29:34</reference>, and Judah; after which she leaves off bearing, <reference osisRef="Gen.29.35">Gen 29:35</reference>. <div eID="gen1394" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1395" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen1395" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1396" type="x-p"/> Then Jacob went on his journey - The original is very remarkable: And Jacob lifted up his feet, and he traveled unto the land of the children of the east. There is a certain cheerfulness marked in the original which comports well with the state of mind into which he had been brought by the vision of the ladder and the promises of God. He now saw that having God for his protector he had nothing to fear, and therefore he went on his way rejoicing. <div eID="gen1396" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1397" type="x-p"/> People of the east - The inhabitants of Mesopotamia and the whole country beyond the Euphrates are called קדם kedem, or easterns, in the sacred writings.
entries.e160435692e61d1be6e9f7a6e9aabdb93c12c13c: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen1397" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1398" type="x-p"/> Three flocks of sheep - צאן tson, small cattle, such as sheep, goats, etc.; See note on <reference osisRef="Gen.12.16">Gen 12:16</reference>. Sheep, in a healthy state, seldom drink in cold and comparatively cold countries: but it was probably different in hot climates. The three flocks, if flocks and not shepherds be meant, which were lying now at the well, did not belong to Laban, but to three other chiefs; for Laban's flock was yet to come, under the care of Rachel, <reference osisRef="Gen.29.6">Gen 29:6</reference>.
entries.3627c4c7478daf055764eb43d82521ae9e385af5: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen1398" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1399" type="x-p"/> All the flocks - Instead of העדרים hadarim, flocks, the Samaritan reads haroim, shepherds; for which reading Houbigant strongly contends, as well in this verse as in <reference osisRef="Gen.29.8">Gen 29:8</reference>. It certainly cannot be said that all the flocks rolled the stone from the well's mouth, and watered the sheep: and yet so it appears to read if we prefer the common Hebrew text to the Samaritan. It is probable that the same reading was originally that of the second verse also. <div eID="gen1399" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1400" type="x-p"/> And put the stone again upon the well's mouth - It is very likely that the stone was a large one, which was necessary to prevent ill-minded individuals from either disturbing the water, or filling up the well; hence a great stone was provided, which required the joint exertions of several shepherds to remove it; and hence those who arrived first waited till all the others were come up, that they might water their respective flocks in concert.
entries.61584865fe1cc5518c53d495023817cff84f8f1e: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen1400" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1401" type="x-p"/> My brethren, whence be ye? - The language of Laban and his family was Chaldee and not Hebrew; (see <reference osisRef="Gen.31.47">Gen 31:47</reference>); but from the names which Leah gave to her children we see that the two languages had many words in common, and therefore Jacob and the shepherds might understand each other with little difficulty. It is possible also that Jacob might have learned the Chaldee or Aramitish language from his mother, as this was his mother's tongue.
entries.af05af490b0cc397cc5479bc53dd973989587197: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen1401" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1402" type="x-p"/> Laban the son of Nahor - Son is here put for grandson, for Laban was the son of Bethuel the son of Nahor.
entries.7af7aeaec6a035ad07ec0759caad90bd35432d30: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen1402" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1403" type="x-p"/> Is he well? - השלום לו hashalom lo? Is there peace to him? Peace among the Hebrews signified all kinds of prosperity. Is he a prosperous man in his family and in his property? And they said, He is well, שלום shalom, he prospers. <div eID="gen1403" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1404" type="x-p"/> Rachel - cometh with the sheep - רחל rachel (the ch sounded strongly guttural) signifies a sheep or ewe; and she probably had her name from her fondness for these animals.
entries.485806e2ce4c6940f56ffcfbcda3587ddcc263c2: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen1404" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1405" type="x-p"/> It is yet high day - The day is but about half run; neither is it time that the cattle should be gathered together - it is surely not time yet to put them into the folds; give them therefore water, and take them again to pasture.
entries.584c5e2a40022dcc7eb1cb067beb552d8e4c4a32: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen1405" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1406" type="x-p"/> We cannot, until all the flocks be gathered together - It is a rule that the stone shall not be removed till all the shepherds and the flocks which have a right to this well be gathered together; then, and not before, we may water the sheep. See note on <reference osisRef="Gen.29.3">Gen 29:3</reference>.
entries.80a09cb748559adc2a8566598476f193e6174378: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen1406" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1407" type="x-p"/> Rachel came with her father's sheep - So we find that young women were not kept concealed in the house till the time they were married, which is the common gloss put on עלמה almah, a virgin, one concealed. Nor was it beneath the dignity of the daughters of the most opulent chiefs to carry water from the well, as in the case of Rebekah; or tend sheep, as in the case of Rachel. The chief property in those times consisted in flocks: and who so proper to take care of them as those who were interested in their safety and increase? Honest labor, far from being a discredit, is an honor both to high and low. The king himself is served by the field; and without it, and the labor necessary for its cultivation, all ranks must perish. Let every son, let every daughter, learn that it is no discredit to be employed, whenever it may be necessary, in the meanest offices, by which the interests of the family may be honestly promoted.
entries.e227dbb7e5c79b83efc99824326ef181d058e682: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen1407" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1408" type="x-p"/> Jacob went near, and rolled the stone - Probably the flock of Laban was the last of those which had a right to the well; that flock being now come, Jacob assisted the shepherds to roll off the stone, (for it is not likely he did it by himself), and so assisted his cousin, to whom he was as yet unknown, to water her flock.
entries.7fa756b5678161788fe4d391bc876b75a7cbad51: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen1408" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1409" type="x-p"/> Jacob kissed Rachel - A simple and pure method by which the primitive inhabitants of the earth testified their friendship to each other, first abused by hypocrites, who pretended affection while their vile hearts meditated terror, (see the case of Joab), and afterwards disgraced by refiners on morals, who, while they pretended to stumble at those innocent expressions of affection and friendship, were capable of committing the grossest acts of impurity. <div eID="gen1409" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1410" type="x-p"/> And lifted up his voice - It may be, in thanksgiving to God for the favor he had shown him, in conducting him thus far in peace and safety. <div eID="gen1410" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1411" type="x-p"/> And wept - From a sense of the goodness of his heavenly Father, and his own unworthiness of the success with which he had been favored. The same expressions of kindness and pure affection are repeated on the part of Laban, <reference osisRef="Gen.29.13">Gen 29:13</reference>.
entries.a6d1efc34f21d57e91f76f7d8457e5123f6efff2: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen1411" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1412" type="x-p"/> My bone and my flesh - One of my nearest relatives.
entries.21a8e25d654f4670639a446c611dd6fb521fd3d6: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen1412" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1413" type="x-p"/> Because thou art my brother, etc. - Though thou art my nearest relative, yet I have no right to thy services without giving thee an adequate recompense. Jacob had passed a whole month in the family of Laban, in which he had undoubtedly rendered himself of considerable service. As Laban, who was of a very saving if not covetous disposition, saw that he was to be of great use to him in his secular concerns, he wished to secure his services, and therefore asks him what wages he wished to have.
entries.9f2fc81674e1d32899b632d6af89ae549af1c39e: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen1413" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1414" type="x-p"/> Leah was tender-eyed - רכות raccoth, soft, delicate, lovely. I believe the word means just the reverse of the signification generally given to it. The design of the inspired writer is to compare both the sisters together, that the balance may appear to be greatly in favor of Rachel. The chief recommendation of Leah was her soft and beautiful eyes; but Rachel was יפת תאר yephath toar, beautiful in her shape, person, mien, and gait, and יפת מראה yephath mareh, beautiful in her countenance. The words plainly signify a fine shape and fine features, all that can be considered as essential to personal beauty. Therefore Jacob loved her, and was willing to become a bond servant for seven years, that he might get her to wife; for in his destitute state he could produce no dowry, and it was the custom of those times for the father to receive a portion for his daughter, and not to give one with her. One of the Hindoo lawgivers says, "A person may become a slave on account of love, or to obtain a wife." The bad system of education by which women are spoiled and rendered in general good for nothing, makes it necessary for the husband to get a dowry with his wife to enable him to maintain her; whereas in former times they were well educated and extremely useful, hence he who got a wife almost invariably got a prize, or as Solomon says, got a good thing.
entries.38cbad6b160160aad308b8a2f8add2c9db11b799: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen1414" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1415" type="x-p"/> And Jacob served seven years for Rachel - In ancient times it appears to have been a custom among all nations that men should give dowries for their wives; and in many countries this custom still prevails. When Shechem asked Dinah for wife, he said, Ask me never so much - dowry and gift, and I will give according as ye shall say unto me. When Eliezer went to get Rebekah for Isaac, he took a profusion of riches with him, in silver, gold, jewels, and raiment, with other costly things, which, when the contract was made, he gave to Rebekah, her mother, and her brothers. David, in order to be Saul's son-in-law, must, instead of a dowry, kill Goliath; and when this was done, he was not permitted to espouse Michal till he had killed one hundred Philistines. The Prophet Hosea bought his wife for fifteen pieces of silver, and a homer and a half of barley. The same custom prevailed among the ancient Greeks, Indians, and Germans. The Romans also had a sort of marriage entitled per coemptionem, "by purchase." The Tartars and Turks still buy their wives; but among the latter they are bought as a sort of slaves. <div eID="gen1415" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1416" type="x-p"/> Herodotus mentions a very singular custom among the Babylonians, which may serve to throw light on Laban's conduct towards Jacob. "In every district they annually assemble all the marriageable virgins on a certain day; and when the men are come together and stand round the place, the crier rising up sells one after another, always bringing forward the most beautiful first; and having sold her for a great sum of gold, he puts up her who is esteemed second in beauty. On this occasion the richest of the Babylonians used to contend for the fairest wife, and to outbid one another. But the vulgar are content to take the ugly and lame with money; for when all the beautiful virgins are sold, the crier orders the most deformed to stand up; and after he has openly demanded who will marry her with a small sum, she is at length given to the man that is contented to marry her with the least. And in this manner the money arising from the sale of the handsome served for a portion to those whose look was disagreeable, or who had any bodily imperfection. A father was not permitted to indulge his own fancy in the choice of a husband for his daughter; neither might the purchaser carry off the woman which he had bought without giving sufficient security that he would live with her as his own wife. Those also who received a sum of money with such as could bring no price in this market, were obliged also to give sufficient security that they would live with them, and if they did not they were obliged to refund the money." Thus Laban made use of the beauty of Rachel to dispose of his daughter Leah, in the spirit of the Babylonian custom, though not in the letter. <div eID="gen1416" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1417" type="x-p"/> And they seemed unto him but a few days - If Jacob had been obliged to wait seven years before he married Rachel, could it possibly be said that they could appear to him as a few days? Though the letter of the text seems to say the contrary, yet there are eminent men who strongly contend that he received Rachel soon after the month was finished, (see <reference osisRef="Gen.29.14">Gen 29:14</reference>), and then served seven years for her, which might really appear but a few days to him, because of his increasing love to her; but others think this quite incompatible with all the circumstances marked down in the text, and on the supposition that Jacob was not now seventy-seven years of age, as most chronologers make him, but only fifty-seven, (see on Genesis 31 (note))., there will be time sufficient to allow for all the transactions which are recorded in his history, during his stay with Laban. As to the incredibility of a passionate lover, as some have termed him, waiting patiently for seven years before he could possess the object of his wishes, and those seven years appearing to him as only a few days, it may be satisfactorily accounted for, they think, two ways: <div eID="gen1417" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1418" type="x-p"/> 1. He had the continual company of his elect spouse, and this certainly would take away all tedium in the case. <div eID="gen1418" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1419" type="x-p"/> 2. Love affairs were not carried to such a pitch of insanity among the patriarchs as they have been in modern times; they were much more sober and sedate, and scarcely ever married before they were forty years of age, and then more for convenience, and the desire of having an offspring, than for any other purpose. <div eID="gen1419" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1420" type="x-p"/> At the very lowest computation Jacob was now fifty-seven, and consequently must have passed those days in which passion runs away with reason. Still, however, the obvious construction of the text shows that he got Rachel the week after he had married Leah.
entries.03f1e21262d53f0e3fc4c692566bc0039b787787: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen1420" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1421" type="x-p"/> My days are fulfilled - My seven years are now completed, let me have my wife, for whom I have given this service as a dowry.
entries.033f999f74886e1cfe3fa2939cb6f87da8073bd7: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen1421" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1422" type="x-p"/> Laban - made a feast - משתה mishteh signifies a feast of drinking. As marriage was a very solemn contract, there is much reason to believe that sacrifices were offered on the occasion, and libations poured out; and we know that on festival occasions a cup of wine was offered to every guest; and as this was drunk with particular ceremonies, the feast might derive its name from this circumstance, which was the most prominent and observable on such occasions.
entries.fa2c26a02d333284d989a2bc7c5de15c6cf6d0f3: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen1422" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1423" type="x-p"/> In the evening - he took Leah his daughter - As the bride was always veiled, and the bride chamber generally dark, or nearly so, and as Leah was brought to Jacob in the evening, the imposition here practiced might easily pass undetected by Jacob, till the ensuing day discovered the fraud.
entries.7298ab5df145f38acd36654bb116bf0b77442514: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen1423" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1424" type="x-p"/> And Laban gave - Zilpah his maid - Slaves given in this way to a daughter on her marriage, were the peculiar property of the daughter; and over them the husband had neither right nor power.
entries.7ee2a521d2e7f10c088fe2dab0ac58ee8af8c835: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen1424" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1425" type="x-p"/> It must not be so done in our country - It was an early custom to give daughters in marriage according to their seniority; and it is worthy of remark that the oldest people now existing, next to the Jews, I mean the Hindoos, have this not merely as a custom, but as a positive law; and they deem it criminal to give a younger daughter in marriage while an elder daughter remains unmarried. Among them it is a high offense, equal to adultery, "for a man to marry while his elder brother remains unmarried, or for a man to give his daughter to such a person, or to give his youngest daughter in marriage while the eldest sister remains unmarried." - Code of Gentoo Laws, chap. xv., sec. 1, p. 204. This was a custom at Mesopotamia; but Laban took care to conceal it from Jacob till after he had given him Leah. The words of Laban are literally what a Hindoo would say on such a subject.
entries.ce65c754ebc422d49a487ae573c2febb1fdf78cb: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen1425" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1426" type="x-p"/> Fulfill her week - The marriage feast, it appears, lasted seven days; it would not therefore have been proper to break off the solemnities to which all the men of the place had been invited, <reference osisRef="Gen.29.22">Gen 29:22</reference>, and probably Laban wished to keep his fraud from the public eye; therefore he informs Jacob that if he will fulfill the marriage week for Leah, he will give him Rachel at the end of it, on condition of his serving seven other years. To this the necessity of the case caused Jacob to agree; and thus Laban had fourteen years' service instead of seven: for it is not likely that Jacob would have served even seven days for Leah, as his affection was wholly set on Rachel, the wife of his own choice. By this stratagem Laban gained a settlement for both his daughters. What a man soweth, that shall he reap. Jacob had before practiced deceit, and is now deceived; and Laban, the instrument of it, was afterwards deceived himself.
entries.57085420dec797f5725ed3e29fee026ad8ccdd92: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen1426" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1427" type="x-p"/> And Jacob did so - and he gave him Rachel - It is perfectly plain that Jacob did not serve seven years more before he got Rachel to wife; but having spent a week with Leah, and in keeping the marriage feast, he then got Rachel, and served afterwards seven years for her. Connections of this kind are now called incestuous; but it appears they were allowable in those ancient times. In taking both sisters, it does not appear that any blame attached to Jacob, though in consequence of it he was vexed by their jealousies. It was probably because of this that the law was made, Thou shalt not take a wife to her sister, to vex her, besides the other in her life-time. After this, all such marriages were strictly forbidden.
entries.cb2022163fa1e3b2ca980714e4fb5975c1f00b05: <hi type="bold">Verse 31</hi> <div eID="gen1427" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1428" type="x-p"/> The Lord saw that Leah was hated - From this and the preceding verse we get the genuine meaning of the word שנא sane, to hate, in certain disputed places in the Scriptures. The word simply signifies a less degree of love; so it is said, <reference osisRef="Gen.29.30">Gen 29:30</reference> : "Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah," i.e., he loved Leah less than Rachel; and this is called hating in <reference osisRef="Gen.29.31">Gen 29:31</reference> : When the Lord saw that Leah was hated - that she had less affection shown to her than was her due, as one of the legitimate wives of Jacob, he opened her womb - he blessed her with children. Now the frequent intercourse of Jacob with Leah (see the following verses) sufficiently proves that he did not hate her in the sense in which this term is used among us; but he felt and showed less affection for her than for her sister. So Jacob have I loved, but Esau have I hated, simply means, I have shown a greater degree of affection for Jacob and his posterity than I have done for Esau and his descendants, by giving the former a better earthly portion than I have given to the latter, and by choosing the family of Jacob to be the progenitors of the Messiah. But not one word of all this relates to the eternal states of either of the two nations. Those who endeavor to support certain peculiarities of their creed by such scriptures as these, do greatly err, not knowing the Scripture, and not properly considering either the sovereignty or the mercy of God.
entries.2581b3a0a38f7ef2c70146c65fbb1503c7e74b29: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen1428" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1429" type="x-p"/> She called his name Reuben - ראובן reuben, literally, see ye or behold a son; for Jehovah hath looked upon, ראה raah, beheld, my affliction; behold then the consequence, I have got a son!
entries.ed0823341360b8b2d763cc144bd29026b609da86: <hi type="bold">Verse 33</hi> <div eID="gen1429" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1430" type="x-p"/> She called his name Simeon - שמעון shimon, hearing; i.e., God had blessed her with another son, because he had heard that she was hated - loved less than Rachel was.
entries.5f41dec34a05e7eb072a856ffa8213402e2afd85: <hi type="bold">Verse 34</hi> <div eID="gen1430" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1431" type="x-p"/> Therefore was his name called Levi - לוי levi, joined; because she supposed that, in consequence of all these children, Jacob would become joined to her in as strong affection, at least, as he was to Rachel. From Levi sprang the tribe of Levites, who instead of the first-born, were joined unto the priests in the service of the sanctuary. See <reference osisRef="Num.18.2">Num 18:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.18.4">Num 18:4</reference>.
entries.d763f77cf3894ce7ff026d44b9f5b1b861496bb6: <hi type="bold">Verse 35</hi> <div eID="gen1431" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1432" type="x-p"/> She called his name Judah - יהודה yehudah, a confessor; one who acknowledges God, and acknowledges that all good comes from his hands, and gives him the praise due to his grace and mercy. From this patriarch the Jews have their name, and could it be now rightly applied to them, it would intimate that they were a people that confess God, acknowledge his bounty, and praise him for his grace. <div eID="gen1432" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1433" type="x-p"/> Left bearing - That is, for a time; for she had several children afterwards. Literally translated, the original תעמד מלדת taamod milledeth - she stood still from bearing, certainly does not convey the same meaning as that in our translation; the one appearing to signify that she ceased entirely from having children; the other, that she only desisted for a time, which was probably occasioned by a temporary suspension of Jacob's company, who appears to have deserted the tent of Leah through the jealous management of Rachel. <div eID="gen1433" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1434" type="x-p"/> The intelligent and pious care of the original inhabitants of the world to call their children by those names which were descriptive of some remarkable event in providence, circumstance of their birth, or domestic occurrence, is worthy, not only of respect, but of imitation. As the name itself continually called to the mind, both of the parents and the child, the circumstance from which it originated, it could not fail to be a lasting blessing to both. How widely different is our custom! Unthinking and ungodly, we impose names upon our offspring as we do upon our cattle; and often the dog, the horse, the monkey, and the parrot, share in common with our children the names which are called Christian! Some of our Christian names, so called, are absurd, others are ridiculous, and a third class impious; these last being taken from the demon gods and goddesses of heathenism. May we hope that the rational and pious custom recommended in the Scriptures shall ever be restored, even among those who profess to believe in, fear, and love God!  <chapter eID="Gen.29"/> <div eID="gen1434" type="x-p"/>

entries.2cff0a4896e9c9fcb55ae69c66a4aa0f5ff99b59: <reference osisRef="Gen.29.1-Gen.29.4">Gen 29:1-4</reference> <div eID="gen348" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen349" type="x-p"/> Arrival in Haran, and Reception by Laban. - Being strengthened in spirit by the nocturnal vision, Jacob proceeded on his journey into “the land of the sons of the East,” by which we are to understand, not so much the Arabian desert, that reaches to the Euphrates, as Mesopotamia, which lies on the other side of that river. For there he saw the well in the field (<reference osisRef="Gen.29.2">Gen 29:2</reference>), by which three flocks were lying, waiting for the arrival of the other flocks of the place, before they could be watered. The remark in <reference osisRef="Gen.29.2">Gen 29:2</reference>, that the stone upon the well’s mouth was large (גּדלה without the article is a predicate), does not mean that the united strength of all the shepherds was required to roll it away, whereas Jacob rolled it away alone (<reference osisRef="Gen.29.10">Gen 29:10</reference>); but only that it was not in the power of every shepherd, much less of a shepherdess like Rachel, to roll it away. Hence in all probability the agreement that had been formed among them, that they would water the flocks together. The scene is so thoroughly in harmony with the customs of the East, both ancient and modern, that the similarity to the one described in Gen 24:11. is by no means strange (vid., Rob. <hi type="italic">Pal.</hi> i. 301, 304, ii. 351, 357, 371). Moreover the well was very differently constructed from that at which Abraham’s servant met with Rebekah. There the water was drawn at once from the (open) well and poured into troughs placed ready for the cattle, as is the case now at most of the wells in the East; whereas here the well was closed up with a stone, and there is no mention of pitchers and troughs. The well, therefore, was probably a cistern dug in the ground, which was covered up or closed with a large stone, and probably so constructed, that after the stone had been rolled away the flocks could be driven to the edge to drink.<note placement="foot">Like the cistern <hi type="italic">Bir Beshat</hi>, described by <hi type="italic">Rosen</hi>., in the valley of Hebron, or those which Robinson found in the desert of Judah (<hi type="italic">Pal.</hi> ii. 165), hollowed out in the great mass of rock, and covered with a large, thick, flat stone, in the middle of which a round hole had been left, which formed the opening of the cistern, and in many cases was closed up with a heavy stone, which it would take two or three men to roll away.</note>
entries.ca174353db1d88d5d90b20892785b47fc5f9b4de: <reference osisRef="Gen.29.5-Gen.29.14">Gen 29:5-14</reference> <div eID="gen349" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen350" type="x-p"/> Jacob asked the shepherds where they lived; from which it is probable that the well was not situated, like that in <reference osisRef="Gen.24.11">Gen 24:11</reference>, in the immediate neighbourhood of the town of Haran; and when they said they were from Haran, he inquired after Laban, the son, i.e., the descendant, of Nahor, and how he was (לו השׁלום: is he well?; and received the reply, “<hi type="italic">Well; and behold Rachel, his daughter, is just coming</hi> (בּאה particip.) <hi type="italic">with the flock</hi>.” When Jacob thereupon told the shepherds to water the flocks and feed them again, for the day was still “great,” - i.e., it wanted a long while to the evening, and was not yet time to drive them in (to the folds to rest for the night) - he certainly only wanted to get the shepherds away from the well, that he might meet with his cousin alone. But as Rachel came up in the meantime, he was so carried away by the feelings of relationship, possibly by a certain love at first sight, that he rolled the stone away from the well, watered her flock, and after kissing her, introduced himself with tears of joyous emotion as her cousin (אביה אחי, brother, i.e., relation of her father) and Rebekah’s son. What the other shepherds thought of all this, is passed over as indifferent to the purpose of the narrative, and the friendly reception of Jacob by Laban is related immediately afterwards. When Jacob had told Laban “<hi type="italic">all these things</hi>,” - i.e., hardly “the cause of his journey, and the things which had happened to him in relation to the birthright” (<hi type="italic">Rosenmüller</hi>), but simply the things mentioned in <reference osisRef="Gen.29.2-Gen.29.12">Gen 29:2-12</reference> - Laban acknowledged him as his relative: “<hi type="italic">Yes, thou art my bone and my flesh</hi>” (cf. <reference osisRef="Gen.2.23">Gen 2:23</reference> and Jdg 9:2); and thereby <hi type="italic">eo ipso</hi> ensured him an abode in his house.
entries.dbc4a1257e59f1768dde722ac2cd1eda0a628921: <reference osisRef="Gen.29.15-Gen.29.20">Gen 29:15-20</reference> <div eID="gen350" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen351" type="x-p"/> Jacob’s Double Marriage. - After a full month (“a month of days,” <reference osisRef="Gen.41.4">Gen 41:4</reference>; Num 11:20, etc.), during which time Laban had discovered that he was a good and useful shepherd, he said to him, “<hi type="italic">Shouldst thou, because thou art my relative, serve me for nothing? fix me thy wages</hi>.” Laban’s selfishness comes out here under the appearance of justice and kindness. To preclude all claim on the part of his sister’s son to gratitude or affection in return for his services, he proposes to pay him like an ordinary servant. Jacob offered to serve him seven years for <hi type="italic">Rachel</hi>, the younger of his two daughters, whom he loved because of her beauty; i.e., just as many years as the week has days, that he might bind himself to a complete and sufficient number of years of service. For the elder daughter, <hi type="italic">Leah</hi>, had weak eyes, and consequently was not so good-looking; since bright eyes, with fire in them, are regarded as the height of beauty in Oriental women. Laban agreed. He would rather give his daughter to him than to a stranger.<note placement="foot">This is the case still with the Bedouins, the Druses, and other Eastern tribes (<hi type="italic">Burckhardt, Voleny, Layard,</hi> and <hi type="italic">Lane</hi></note>. <div eID="gen351" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen352" type="x-p"/> Jacob’s proposal may be explained, partly on the ground that he was not then in a condition to give the customary dowry, or the usual presents to relations, and partly also from the fact that his situation with regard to Esau compelled him to remain some time with Laban. The assent on the part of Laban cannot be accounted for from the custom of selling daughters to husbands, for it cannot be shown that the purchase of wives was a general custom at that time; but is to be explained solely on the ground of Laban’s selfishness and avarice, which came out still more plainly afterwards. To Jacob, however, the seven years seemed but “<hi type="italic">a few days, because he loved Rachel</hi>.” This is to be understood, as <hi type="italic">C. a Lapide</hi> observes, “not <hi type="italic">affective</hi>, but <hi type="italic">appretiative</hi>,” i.e., in comparison with the reward to be obtained for his service.
entries.48c61e9ca28c434da8d032ba6b1f431481c650fd: <reference osisRef="Gen.29.21-Gen.29.24">Gen 29:21-24</reference> <div eID="gen352" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen353" type="x-p"/> But when Jacob asked for his reward at the expiration of this period, and according to the usual custom a great marriage feast had been prepared, instead of Rachel, Laban took his elder daughter Leah into the bride-chamber, and Jacob went in unto her, without discovering in the dark the deception that had been practised. Thus the overreacher of Esau was overreached himself, and sin was punished by sin.
entries.fe1e969f55bdde3e0bd214708d1abf2f0b3a834f: <reference osisRef="Gen.29.25-Gen.29.26">Gen 29:25-26</reference> <div eID="gen353" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen354" type="x-p"/> But when Jacob complained to Laban the next morning of his deception, he pleaded the custom of the country: כּן יעשׂה לא, “<hi type="italic">it is not accustomed to be so in our place, to give the younger before the first-born</hi>.” A perfectly worthless excuse; for if this had really been the custom in Haran as in ancient India and elsewhere, he ought to have told Jacob of it before. But to satisfy Jacob, he promised him that in a week he would give him the younger also, if he would serve him seven years longer for her.
entries.1af1ffe242c582228acdd28e521127d0cc0d3fc9: <reference osisRef="Gen.29.27-Gen.29.30">Gen 29:27-30</reference> <div eID="gen354" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen355" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">Fulfil her week;</hi>” i.e., let Leah’s marriage-week pass over. The wedding feast generally lasted a week (cf. Jdg 14:12; <reference osisRef="Job.11.19">Job 11:19</reference>). After this week had passed, he received Rachel also: two wives in eight days. To each of these Laban gave one maid-servant to wait upon her; less, therefore, than Bethuel gave to his daughter (<reference osisRef="Gen.24.61">Gen 24:61</reference>). - This bigamy of Jacob must not be judged directly by the Mosaic law, which prohibits marriage with two sisters at the same time (<reference osisRef="Lev.18.18">Lev 18:18</reference>), or set down as incest (<hi type="italic">Calvin</hi>, etc.), since there was no positive law on the point in existence then. At the same time, it is not to be justified on the ground, that the blessing of God made it the means of the fulfilment of His promise, viz., the multiplication of the seed of Abraham into a great nation. Just as it had arisen from Laban’s deception and Jacob’s love, which regarded outward beauty alone, and therefore from sinful infirmities, so did it become in its results a true school of affliction to Jacob, in which God showed to him, by many a humiliation, that such conduct as his was quite unfitted to accomplish the divine counsels, and thus condemned the ungodliness of such a marriage, and prepared the way for the subsequent prohibition in the law.
entries.70e45c5424eadd8be4063b94db852129c92d57ab: <reference osisRef="Gen.29.31-Gen.29.35">Gen 29:31-35</reference> <div eID="gen355" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen356" type="x-p"/> Leah’s First Sons. - Jacob’s sinful weakness showed itself even after his marriage, in the fact that he loved Rachel more than Leah; and the chastisement of God, in the fact that the hated wife was blessed with children, whilst Rachel for a long time remained unfruitful. By this it was made apparent once more, that the origin of Israel was to be a work not of nature, but of grace. Leah had four sons in rapid succession, and gave them names which indicated her state of mind: (1) <hi type="italic">Reuben</hi>, “see, a son!” because she regarded his birth as a pledge that <hi type="italic">Jehovah</hi> had graciously looked upon her misery, for now her husband would love her; (2) <hi type="italic">Simeon</hi>, i.e., “hearing,” for <hi type="italic">Jehovah</hi> had heard, i.e., observed that she was hated; (3) <hi type="italic">Levi</hi>, i.e., attachment, for she hoped that this time, at least, after she had born three sons, her husband would become attached to her, i.e., show her some affection; (4) <hi type="italic">Judah</hi> (יהוּדה, <hi type="italic">verbal</hi>, of the <hi type="italic">fut. hoph</hi>. of ידה), i.e., praise, not merely the praised one, but the one for whom <hi type="italic">Jehovah</hi> is praised. After this fourth birth there was a pause (<reference osisRef="Gen.29.31">Gen 29:31</reference>), that she might not be unduly lifted up by her good fortune, or attribute to the fruitfulness of her own womb what the faithfulness of <hi type="italic">Jehovah</hi>, the covenant God had bestowed upon her.  <chapter eID="Gen.29"/> <div eID="gen356" type="x-p"/>

entries.1b6bcdeca1c81ab588d1400e049055c0b34952ae: <div annotateRef="Bible:Gen.29.1" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Gen.29.1" sID="gen3798" type="section"/> <div sID="gen3799" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">1.</hi> <hi type="italic">Then Jacob went on his journey</hi> <note n="62"> <div sID="gen3800" type="x-p"/> <foreign xml:lang="la">Et levavit Iahacob pedes suos</foreign> And Jacob lifted up his feet. See margin of English Bible. This is a correct translation of the Hebrew <foreign xml:lang="he">ישא רגליו</foreign>, (<hi type="italic">yissa</hi> <hi type="italic">reglav</hi>.) “The phrase is emphatic, and implies that he traveled on briskly and cheerfully, notwithstanding his age, being refreshed in his spirit by the recent manifestation of the Divine favor.” — <hi type="italic">Bush</hi>. — <hi type="italic">Ed</hi><div eID="gen3800" type="x-p"/> </note> Moses now relates the arrival of Jacob in Mesopotamia, and the manner in which he was received by his uncle; and although the narration may seem superfluous, it yet contains nothing but what is useful to be known; for he commends the extraordinary strength of Jacob’s faith, when he says, that he lifted up his feet to come into an unknown land. Again, he would have us to consider the providence of God, which caused Jacob to fall in with the shepherds, by whom he was conducted to the home he sought; for this did not happen accidentally, but he was guided by the hidden hand of God to that place; and the shepherds, who were to instruct and confirm him respecting all things, were brought thither at the same time. Therefore, whenever we may wander in uncertainty through intricate windings, we must contemplate, with eyes of faith, the secret providence of God which governs us and our affairs, and leads us to unexpected results.<div eID="gen3799" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Gen.29.1" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen3798" osisID="Gen.29.1" type="section"/>
entries.9df032382b37fb7837107ee15d790a46f0e3ad38: <div annotateRef="Bible:Gen.29.4" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Gen.29.4" sID="gen3801" type="section"/> <div sID="gen3802" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">4.</hi> <hi type="italic">My brethren, whence be ye?</hi> The great frankness of that age appears in this manner of meeting together; for, though the fraternal name is often abused by dishonest and wicked men, it is yet not to be doubted that friendly intercourse was then more faithfully cultivated than it is now. This was the reason why Jacob salutes unknown men as brethren, undoubtedly according to received custom. Frugality also is apparent, in that Rachel sometimes pays attention to the flock; for, since Laban abounds with servants, how does it happen that he employs his own daughter in a vile and sordid service, except that it was deemed disgraceful to educate children in idleness, softness, and indulgence? Whereas, on the contrary, at this day, since ambition, pride, and refinement, have rendered manners effeminate, the care of domestic concerns is held in such contempt, that women, for the most part, are ashamed of their proper office.
